Abstract 
The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with simulation-based methods is transforming predictive 
mechanical design by enabling faster, data-driven, and adaptive decision-making. Traditional approaches 
like finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are computationally expensive 
and often limited in handling highly nonlinear or multi-parameter systems. AI, particularly machine 
learning and deep learning, offers a breakthrough by learning implicit relationships from large datasets to 
create surrogate models that rapidly evaluate design alternatives at lower costs. Reinforcement learning 
enables autonomous exploration of design spaces, while evolutionary algorithms and generative design 
assist in discovering innovative structures and material distributions that meet strength, weight, and 
efficiency targets. 
Reliability is enhanced through uncertainty quantification and probabilistic modelling, which predict 
design behaviour under varying conditions. Coupled with multi-physics simulations, AI accelerates 
optimization for aerodynamics, thermal management, fatigue life prediction, and additive manufacturing. 
Digital twins powered by sensor data further support predictive maintenance by forecasting failures and 
extending lifecycle performance. Additionally, combining AI with high-performance computing (HPC) 
enables real-time optimization of complex systems in aerospace, automotive, robotics, and energy sectors. 
Future progress lies in hybrid AI-physics models that ensure predictive accuracy while preserving 
fundamental engineering laws, driving smarter, sustainable, and more reliable designs. 
 
Introduction 
Definition of Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its relevance to mechanical design and optimization 
Artificial intelligence (AI) is when a computer system or program can simulate the functions of the human 
brain, such as thinking, learning, making decisions, and solving problems. Using methods such as machine 
learning, evolutionary algorithms, neural networks, natural language processing, etc., artificial intelligence 
systems can analyze a volume of data and extract patterns that would otherwise be impossible for mankind 
and also produce predictive results. From an engineering point of view, AI isn't just a computational tool, 
it is a paradigm change that speeds the pace of innovation and will change the way we solve complex 
problems. Artificial intelligence (AI) is the strategic tool for designing and optimizing machines for 
efficient, reliable and optimum performance [1]. Traditional design processes are typically iterative, time-
consuming and expensive from a computational perspective: different design configurations must be 
tested with serial simulations and analyses. AI is answering these questions by becoming a predictive & 
optimization module. For example, machine learning can be applied to predict simulation results (as 
surrogates to computationally expensive finite element or fluid dynamics models) for quick evaluation of 
the entire design space [2]. Reinforcement learning techniques and evolutionary engineering are utilized

Background on predictive mechanical design and optimization 
Predictive mechanical design and optimization represents a paradigm shift from traditional engineering 
methods by synergistically embedding data-based modeling and simulation as well as high performance 
computing in the prediction and design optimization process. Traditionally, the mechanical design process 
has relied on iterative loops of computational simulation (finite element analysis [FEA], computational 
fluid dynamics [CFD]) that are followed by physical prototyping for design optimization. These methods 
have been proven to work, but are computationally costly and time consuming [5]. Predictive design aims 
to help eliminate the time necessary to achieve this; by predicting the behavior of mechanical components 
and systems prior to physical proofout, engineers gain the ability to quickly explore a significantly larger 
number of design variation possibilities. At the heart of predictive design is the capability to use 
mathematical models and algorithms that represent the connections between design variables and 
performance outcomes. Optimization then focuses on the search for such relationships with the goal of 
finding the best set of trade-offs between multiple objectives (e.g. minimum weight and maximum strength 
or minimum cost and maximum reliability). For mechanical systems that contain competing effects, multi-
objective optimization methods are used routinely [6]. They are more powerful through improved 
computers and improved algorithms: the problems they can solve are both more complex and realistic. Of 
particular interest are newly emerging trends for the integration of artificial intelligence and machine 
learning into predictive design and optimization workflows. Several global modeling technologies use 
historical and simulation data to build surrogate models (very small computationally inexpensive 
approximations to complete simulations) to effectively recover most modeling time to analysis. 
Furthermore, we can implement intelligent optimisation schemes which efficiently search large design 
spaces with machine learning algorithms, and find new solutions that would not be found from traditional 
searches. Furthermore, mathematical methods for the prediction of the failure behaviour and maintenance 
requirements of an optimised life cycle management of a mechanical system are presented. As a 
consequence, predictive mechanical design and optimisation has become an important tool for modern 
engineering industries such as aerospace, automotive, robotics and renewable energy applications, helping 
to innovate whilst limiting development time and cost [7].

for mechanical engineers, providing intelligent solutions that can help them address complex design 
challenges more effectively through a combination of domain knowledge and data-driven insights. The 
result of Hertzsprung's contribution is reduced development time, lower costs, improved product reliability 
and the ability to bring products to market quickly in a wide range of industries, including aerospace 
vehicles, automobiles, robotics and renewable energy. If desired, the process may also involve specialized 
artificial intelligence techniques being applied to mechanical design and optimization. Artificial 
Intelligence (AI) has become an invaluable tool for the transformation of the engineering profession by 
creating smarter, more efficient, precise and novel methods for engineering design and optimization [11]. 
Conventional mechanical design requires too many computationally intensive design iterations to reach 
an optimum structural-functional performance. AI will address these issues by using more accurate 
algorithms and models for better predictions based on existing published data from design and simulation, 
by doing linear operations faster through automation, by detecting new solutions outside of what is already 
known. On a technological level, the largest impact of AI is in generative design, in which an algorithm 
can autonomously produce thousands of design alternatives within defined constraints of weight, strength, 
environmental conditions, etc. This allows engineers to experiment with new designs that provide 
maximum efficiency and maximum performance, while requiring minimum material. Plus, ML allows for 
the simulation of expensive tests (time and cost) that would otherwise hinder the iterations of a design. 
Apart from design, predictive maintenance and life cycle optimization, AI can also be integrated with 
digital twins - digital models of a machine that include real-time data. "This will help to accurately predict 
failure and reduce downtime and maintenance costs." AI is also improving computer-aided design (CAD) 
software for human users by catching potential design errors sooner, enabling so-called rapid prototyping

Objective and scope of the review article 
Therefore, the objective of this review article is to report and summarize the achievements, approaches 
and applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) to predictive mechanical design and optimization. Artificial 
intelligence (AI) is a powerful technology that can collaborate with conventional computers to enable 
complex mechanical systems with increased complexity and associated high demands for efficiency, 
accuracy, and novelty. With this review, we aim to provide the reader with the best possible description 
of the evolving predictive design and optimisation approach when AI-based predictive techniques 
(machine learning, deep learning, evolutionary algorithms and digital twins) are utilised. More concretely, 
the article will illustrate how AI methods accelerate design change by building surrogates (reduced 
footprint) that can be used for multi-objective optimisation (e.g. weight, strength and cost) or generative 
design (find the best structure/material distribution). It also looks at how AI can be applied to optimise 
lifecycle, predictive maintenance and just-in-time viewing with AI-based digital twins. The authors also 
share case studies and use cases from technology in high-risk industries such as aerospace, automotive, 
robotics and renewable energy, as well as the impact of artificial intelligence on specific areas such as 
improved performance and sustainability [2].The article also highlights the limitations and capabilities of 
AI in mechanical design, such as challenges related to data quality, model interpretability, and integration 
with physical simulation. In addition to providing an overview of the current state of the literature and 
emerging methodology in regards to AI, this review also notes gaps and opportunities for future research 
to further advance and expand the reliability, scale, and utility of AI in engineering workflows. Finally, 
we hope this review can help researchers, engineers, and practitioners who want to leverage the power of 
AI for transformative predictive mechanical design and optimization, as well as accelerating the pace of 
invention and innovation, lowering costs, and enabling next-generation mechanical systems [13]. 
 
Overview of AI Techniques Used in Mechanical Design and Optimization 
Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) algorithms 
As subsets of Artificial Intelligence (AI), Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning (DL) are playing a 
key role in mechanical design and manufacturing optimization, helping us make data-driven decisions in 
a predictive and automated fashion. Machine learning (ML) algorithms provide a new paradigm for 
systems to learn from their history without being explicitly programmed by a human - so engineers can 
extract correlations, make predictions and optimize design variables. In mechanical engineering, ML 
techniques (e.g., regression, decision tree, support vector machines, and ensemble techniques) are used to 
construct surrogate models that could replace computationally expensive simulation tasks based on 
computational fluid dynamics or finite element analysis. With the surrogate modelling, we save a lot of 
time in analysing the design alternatives [14]. ML can also be used to achieve multi-objective optimization 
that balances tradeoffs between competing design objectives (such as strength/lightweight/cost trades, for 
example). Finally, ML is a key tool for predictive maintenance: ML models based on the data collected 
by the sensors in real time can provide an estimate of the moment when the equipment will fail, and 
interventions can be planned to minimize or avoid both down time and operating costs. The next level of

will increase the performance of systems, including aerospace engineering, car engineering, robot, 
renewable energy production systems, etc., and will reduce the cost and accelerate the innovation speed 
in the mechanical engineering design process [15]. 
Optimization techniques (e.g., genetic algorithms, particle swarm optimization) 
In recent years, Genetic Algorithm (GA) and Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) have been widely used 
for mechanical design, so as to solve the complicated engineering optimization problems. GA is an 
abstraction of ideas from natural selection. It has been generated by the evolution of a population of 
candidate solutions (using the selection, crossover and mutation operators). The fitness function is defined 
as both the quality of individual PS candidates. Generative Adaptation (GA) will explore large problem 
spaces in search of solutions that move toward an optimum, and is used for multi-objective and nonlinear 
problems (for which good solutions simply can't be found unless you explore large problem spaces). In 
the field of mechanical engineering, GA is used as an optimum design tool for structural design or for the 
selection of material parameters or process parameters that are not possible with classical approaches[16]. 
PSO is inspired by flocking bird behavior or schooling fish behavior So it has a swarm of particles that 
are all possible solutions. Particles pass through the solution space by modulation of the velocity with a 
function of the best position of the particle and the best position of the swarm as a whole. Particle swarm 
optimization (PSO) can be adopted to solve the continuous multi-objective problem and the computational 
efficiency and implementation simplicity are better than that of genetic algorithms (GA). Mechanical 
applications - machining optimisation, shape optimisation, topology optimisation, control optimisation - 
Both are easily generalised to complex, nonlinear, multi-modal problems, and are typically augmented 
with other algorithms to improve performance. For such a type of optimization problem, Gaussian artificial 
neural network (GANN) outperforms the global search capability of GA and the Particle Swarm 
Optimisation (PSO) algorithm. By offering a framework for efficiently exploring large design spaces 
while simultaneously considering multiple performance objectives, optimization techniques are becoming 
an invaluable feature of predictive mechanical design to realize new innovations in devices and products 
[17]. 
Other AI techniques 
Expert Systems, Fuzzy Logic - have important applications in mechanical engineering. Expert Systems –  
rules-based reasoning takes the place of human expert knowledge to help make design decisions, 
diagnostics, failure analysis, and supervisory control. They formalize expert knowledge into an 
understandable structure to best help decision-makers solve problems or identify problems that will yield 
accurate decisions for complex systems in an efficient manner. Fuzzy logic represents numbers in an 
imprecise form, using approximate reasoning, while handling imprecision, uncertainty and vagueness;

Applications of AI in Predictive Mechanical Design 
Predictive modelling and simulation 
In mechanical engineering allows computational models of mechanical systems to be developed to predict 
their behaviour under all types of operating conditions. These models are built by predicting performance 
(stress, deformations, thermal response, failure modes, etc.) from information gathered by sensors, 
experimental tests and/or simulation measurements. Predictive models help engineers effortlessly run an 
enormous amount of parametric analysis in a fraction of the time, without relying solely on time-
consuming physical prototyping or lengthy simulations for design optimization [11]. Predictive modelling 
- combinations of machine learning and traditional physics-based simulation that enables faster design 
cycles closer to the truth. This is so engineers can make decisions in real time by quickly modeling the 
effects of a design change, or of operating conditions. Predictive simulation is adopted for the life-cycle 
management as well by predicting the maintenance needs while reducing the down time by early 
anticipation of failures. Ultimately, the ability to predict how a mechanical design will perform, using 
predictive modeling and simulation, saves money, allows higher productivity, and enables innovation by 
generating actionable insight and supporting data-driven decision making throughout product 
development [11]. 
Design space exploration and optimization 
Design space exploration and optimization (DSEO) is a field of research that computationally explores a 
large solution space defined by design variables in order to find designs most favorable for satisfying the 
performance objectives. This then saves time for the engineers as it allows them to make tradeoffs between 
competing objectives such as strength, weight, cost and efficiency. In addition to the process of trying to 
find the solution by manually experimenting with hundreds of different things, you can also search in 
high-dimensional spaces and try to find points that look promising by using some clever algorithms [19]. 
Optimization-based algorithms for finding optimal/near-optimal designs are used during design space 
exploration to speed up the search by narrowing down the design space to those designs that fulfill the 
constraints. Such an approach would shorten the time to market by limiting the number of iterations, and 
by allowing decisions to be made earlier in the design process. Often, software will provide a more 
interactive tool that allows designers to take an active role, not only in manually controlling the process, 
but also in automated optimization while retaining a certain level of control all the way through to final 
design and production [20]. Applications include all manner of mechanical devices ranging from 
aerospace components and automotive parts to HVAC systems that demand better performance, lighter 
materials and lower costs. The trend for future optimization is a closer integration of optimization and 
design tools and the use of AI in order to handle increasingly more difficult design spaces [11]. 
Material selection and properties prediction 
Material selection and prediction of properties are important for mechanical engineering problems, in 
order to guarantee the selection of materials that fulfill their function, are of an affordable cost, and are 
ecologically sustainable [21]. Artificial intelligence (AI)-based techniques, particularly machine learning 
(ML), have transformed the process by providing effective analysis of large quantities of data about

Case studies and examples 
Below are some examples and case studies of predictive mechanical design and optimization applications 
of Artificial Intelligence: 
1. Turbomachinery Design Optimization 
quasi-real-time turbomachinery component performance map construction using machine learning for 
complex turbomachinery components With the wealth of cost and performance data available in a 
turbomachinery design, this approach will enable engineers to save enormous amounts of time and money 
spent in design space exploration by allowing them to rapidly and easily perform design variation and 
operating condition queries [24]. 
2. Heat Exchanger Performance Prediction 
Another example of such real-time applications is the predictive modeling optimization done for heat 
exchangers of various topologies using AI based predictive models. This allows an accelerated design

an improved heat transfer efficiency [25]. 
3. Design of automobile chassis 
The problem of chassis design of car was solved by using the machine learning algorithm. Further, by 
finding the most efficient (and cheapest) designs in a process where thousands of design variations were

4. Aerospace Wing Optimization 
AI predictive (extreme edge cases) modeling for patterning optimization of aircraft wing geometry to 
minimize aerodynamic drag and fuel burn improving development time and allowing higher aircraft

5. Consumer Electronics Design 
Artificial Intelligence was applied to smartphone casing design to optimize the design based on users' 
preferences, manufacturing constraints and market trends. Thus, as it were, from the base have been 
developed three-dimensional products corresponding to the requirements of the consumer that are biggest 
ergonomically, aesthetically and economically convenient products. These are just a few examples of how 
AI techniques make mechanical design more effective, efficient, performant, and innovative across the 
broadest array of businesses [28].

Challenges and Limitations of AI in Mechanical Design and Optimization 
Data quality and availability 
The availability of data and data quality is one of the biggest challenges at the moment for AI in mechanical 
design and optimization. A lack of relevant, quality datasets, inadequate or incomplete data structures 
and/or models that lead to inaccurate or unusable design recommendations, and models that just don't paint 
a realistic picture are common roadblocks to accelerating AI application and achieving impact. Data 
Quality Problems - Mechanical design projects generate all kinds of data (i.e., CAD files, simulation 
outputs, sensor records, material specifications), but this information is frequently inconsistent, 
incomplete, and incorrect. Inconsistent data and formats: Data from different sources and in different 
formats is often difficult for AI to consume, and can introduce biases or noise into the training data [29]. 
Keep data representative, validated and up to date - DSSA data is huge, complex and often proprietary 
which can make this tricky. AI design requires large volumes of representative data covering a wide-range 
of use cases and design constraints. Too many organizations do not have access to or share enough quality 
data because privacy laws, trade-secrets or different data systems prevent them from seeing or aggregating 
data. Furthermore, the lack of standardization of datasets across repositories like Smarter Balanced 
Assessment Consortium in the US or ISO/IEC 26 and ISO 47494 in Europe makes optimization and 
prediction modeling more difficult and time-consuming in developing innovations for mechanical 
engineering. Design and Optimization Remote Impacts: For the case of design problems, limited data 
availability affects the generalization performance of AI negatively, and poor data availability restricts the 
scope of application of optimization algorithms. In order to ensure that these humanity-like machines 
won't fool the network engineers often have to manually validate or complement AI outputs, restricting 
the maximum possible use of automation and the full capacity of predictive design. Leveraging AI makes 
this kind of transformation possible in mechanical design and optimization, but these data issues have to 
be addressed first [30]. 
Interpretability and explainability of AI models 
Interpretability and explainability Companies need to ensure that the AI models they deploy for 
mechanical design and optimization are interpretable, so that their decisions can be understood, trusted, 
and validated by engineers and stakeholders. Interpretability Challenges - Most of the advanced AI models 
(especially deep learning and generative AI) are deployed as "black boxes," where the rationale of design 
recommendations or optimization suggestions can't be explained outright [29]. Mechanistic 
interpretability seeks to perform model de novo (reverse engineering) to extract the relationship between 
internal representation and physical/engineering properties, but has so far failed to show in practice how 
it is possible to extract complex reasoning for complex problems. Advances in explainability: 
Explainability techniques have evolved from relatively lightweight post-hoc rationales like feature 
importance to inherently transparent architectures that can justify their reasoning processes in real-time. 
These range from interactive explanations tailored to the skill level of the technical vs. non-technical 
audience, to visualization of reasoning logic, as well as the incorporation of interpretable audit trails for 
AI-based designs. Impact and Importance explainability can help enable trust, regulatory compliance, and 
design accountability. As AI-enabled solutions expand throughout various critical workflows (not the least 
of which are safety and regulatory requirements surrounding standard petroleum processes), transparent 
AI allows engineers to provide supporting decision-making, mitigate risk, and ensure alignment with a 
company's business practices. Keeping it simple - Explanable models are therefore fast becoming strategic 
requirements for organisations using AI in engineering domains [29].

Computational resources and efficiency 
Data-intensive - a mechanical design optimization AI model is usually consumed by data, so enlarging 
performance for data-intensive models is often impossible when using a training-based and simulation-
based model. Computational needs: resources, time, performance, etc. Deep learning algorithms, 
generative models, and large-scale simulations require high-performance computing resources, such as 
high-performance GPUs, cloud clusters, and specialized software packages. Initial investment: The initial 
investment in establishing this infrastructure, which includes hardware, software, and training for 
employees, can be a barrier for smaller organizations. Additionally, these materials have ongoing 
operating costs and as such require ongoing investment for maintenance [30]. Efficiency tradeoffs - While 
the ability to quickly generate copies of AI models to iterate on design and provide feedback can make 
your work more efficient during the iteration phase, this capability can become less efficient as datasets 
grow in size or you increase the complexity of your designs. For optimization and multi-objective 
optimization, the simulation time steps are increased a lot as the energy consumption, the processing time 
and the memory requirement are greatly increased [29]. AI system compatibility: AI incompatibility with 
existing mechanical systems can be another source of inefficiency, especially on legacy systems where 
there might not be a pre-existing solution for AI retrofitting yet. Industry Trends Solutions are more 
efficient (better algorithm, etc) or cheaper to train AI models (cost down almost 10x/year, so not an issue 
anymore) However, enterprise and government organizations would do well to continuously tweak 
compute strategies, calibrate models, and install infrastructure apertures for engineering challenges that 
will yield the best performance [31]. 
Integration with existing design and optimization workflows 
While artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming the way teams innovate, collaborate, and get products out 
the door, there are technical and organizational barriers to implementing AI in existing design and 
optimization workflows - especially in mechanical engineering. Integration Approaches: This is why AI 
is often a smart wrapper around ME - because, at the end of the day, ME is nothing else than a set of tools 
(CAD, CAE, PLM, etc) with an intelligent decision-making process behind this product innovation. And 
the latest CAD, like Solidworks, Fusion 360 or Onshape are already fitted with an AI system for generative 
design, automatic validation, layout optimization and real-time simulation. Instead of replacing 
engineering applications, AI complements existing applications, automating parts of the work that do not 
require human intervention (such as rules checking, drawing checks), providing feedback quickly and 
allowing engineers to re-order parts while making changes [32]. With the supporting data, the leading 
advantages of Intelligent Automated Workflow Design are: Greater throughput, increased engineering 
iteration speed, operational excellence without increasing headcount. Automated validation and near-
instant feedback on products, removes delays, rework and late-stage design mistakes AI application can 
also allow knowledge capture from across the organisation, through systematic codification of expert 
rules, decision criteria, and best practices that can subsequently be applied in decision making[33]. 
Challenges: Generic to AI, but some challenges include: quality of data, integrations to legacy systems, 
resistance to change, pilots to solve point solutions Our experience is that strategic adoption must be top-
down with target drawing validation, automatic re-use of components, and engineers on board from day 
one to adapt workflows for a menu-driven approach - but with human interaction always remaining the 
most important aspect of design oversight. Consistency, compliance, and agility are all key components 
to long-term scaling and success. In the future, orchestration will replace automation - allowing engineers 
to monitor and control hyper-intelligent agents that are incorporated into coordinated model-based

Future Directions and Opportunities 
Emerging trends and technologies (e.g., physics-informed neural networks, transfer learning) 
Conversely, trends and technologies like Transfer Learning and Physics-Informed Neural Networks 
(PINNs) are being widely adopted in the field of mechanical engineering as tools to reimagine AI-enabled 
design and optimization workflows. Physics-informed neural network (PINN) PINNs incorporate physics 
(which is also represented as differential equations) into the training of the neural network, so that the AI 
making the prediction is subjected to these constraints. Issues of limited or noisy data are also addressed 
by introducing physics into the loss function, producing results that are more believable and easier to 
interpret in models of mechanical systems [34].

with improved accuracy and throughput Transfer learning will re-purpose the pre-trained models for new 
mechanical engineering tasks, performing these tasks more accurately and with less training data and

Abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) with simulation-based methods is transforming predictive mechanical design by enabling faster, data-driven, and adaptive decision-making. Traditional approaches like finite element analysis (FEA) and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) are computationally expensive and often limited in handling highly nonlinear or multi-parameter systems. AI, particularly machine learning and deep learning, offers a breakthrough by learning implicit relationships from large datasets to create surrogate models that rapidly evaluate design alternatives at lower costs. Reinforcement learning enables autonomous exploration of design spaces, while evolutionary algorithms and generative design assist in discovering innovative structures and material distributions that meet strength, weight, and efficiency targets. Reliability is enhanced through uncertainty quantification and probabilistic modelling, which predict design behaviour under varying conditions. Coupled with multi-physics simulations, AI accelerates optimization for aerodynamics, thermal management, fatigue life prediction, and additive manufacturing. Digital twins powered by sensor data further support predictive maintenance by forecasting failures and extending lifecycle performance. Additionally, combining AI with high-performance computing (HPC) enables real-time optimization of complex systems in aerospace, automotive, robotics, and energy sectors. Future progress lies in hybrid AI-physics models that ensure predictive accuracy while preserving fundamental engineering laws, driving smarter, sustainable, and more reliable designs.
